1: Central has established a monthly material-output benchmark.
For material we can't reliably predict?
The target uses the pilot's most productive week.
That was the week a damper failed. I don't intend to break another one for the chart.
2: They projected a monthly target from one good batch. That's not a forecast.
The calculation is consistent. The assumption is weak.
Does the number come with the replacement parts we were promised?
It comes with priority consideration. Which is how we ended up discussing it at all.
3: The bracket is still temporary. I can keep checking it, but I can't make the replacement appear.
They've tied accelerated procurement to the new target.
That's a dirty trick. It's also a part I want.
That's exactly why I haven't just said no.
4: Our pilot terms say real work comes first. The target doesn't change that.
It changes which work central will praise.
And if they pay us for more material, they'll start treating every reading as a success or failure.
Does that mean we lose the quiet room if people aren't miserable enough?
That's what I'm worried you'll have to keep saying.
5: The maintenance schedule and output target can be compared on the same calendar.
Move a small, legitimate check forward. We might get the part review sooner.
We shouldn't schedule repairs because they might produce residue.
We aren't inventing repairs. We're changing when we do one.
The first adjustment has no apparent conflict.
That isn't the same as no conflict.
6: Zib, could the vibration check be done tomorrow instead?
Physically, yes. But tomorrow already belongs to another set of people.
I can ask about shifting the room schedule.
It's not the room. It's the dock handoff and the tools we're using.
I'll take responsibility for the change.
7: Don't rush because headquarters has put a star next to this job.
I didn't know there were stars. I was hoping for lunch.
The first trace is a reading, not a reward.
Vibration check is complete. Parameters are normal.
Interesting. But we haven't proved why it appeared.
8: The early check went well. The part request moved to priority review.
I was relieved until I saw you looking at next week's calendar.
No. But I remember what you said when we first sent that material report.
9: Could we move the conveyor service forward as well?
It's a bigger job. We'd have to take the cargo lane apart.
There's a delivery scheduled the following morning.
We can finish before it arrives. I'll confirm the window.
10: The samples are different sizes even with similar work. That's not a controllable output.
I know the target is shaky. The replacement part isn't imaginary.
I want the part too. I just don't want us to pretend the sample isn't telling us something inconvenient.
Write it down. I'll read it after the conveyor check.
11: Our projected output is ahead of target.
At least the earlier maintenance seems to have bought us room.
Funny. I'm looking at the same calendar, and we've lost the room we needed for Dock Two.
The cargo slot is tomorrow. We have time.
12: How long before the conveyor is back in service?
Long enough that I don't like seeing the Dock Two shipment already on the approach list.
You confirmed the planned time. The coupling didn't sign your calendar.
Show me what's left to do.
13: The outer dock is reporting an early arrival.
Conveyor is still isolated. Nobody's moving cargo through this lane.
I can help with the interlock readings.
I can give the pilot an updated estimate, not a guessed one.
Don't let the output target affect the repair steps.
It already affected when we started. Let's not let it affect how we finish.
14: They've asked if we're having an emergency.
It's a scheduling error, not an emergency. I can hear them asking for a shorter word.
I brought the service forward. I thought the lane would be clear.
Well, the lane isn't. They're going to want to know when it will be.
15: Finish isolation safely, clear the lane, and take the shipment. Forget today's target.
The target isn't the part that's broken. It's the reason we're in the way.
I can give Dock Two five minutes if you can actually give me five minutes.
I'm updating the arrival crew now.
16: Conveyor's restored. Check the interlock once more.
Dock Two outer latch is waiting. We've got one chance to look organized.
They don't need organized. They need a working dock.
Finally, something we all agree on.
I'll explain the delay. To the crew, not just the computer.
17: The material-output metric still shows us ahead.
And the delivery was delayed because I moved a service job to improve it.
The two results exist in different reports.
That's the problem. Put the actual work schedule back the way it belongs.
18: The dock crew lost an hour because we wanted a better graph.
Because I wanted the replacement parts. That's why I made the call.
Wanting the parts wasn't wrong. Making the rest of us absorb the change without asking was.
I know. The schedule is back. I'll speak to the dock crew.
19: The honest material forecast misses central's target.
Even though the station's repairs and response times improved.
Put them beside each other. I want whoever reads this to see both.
That won't make them like the numbers.
No. But it will make them understand whose work the numbers interrupted.
20: I moved the conveyor service early. Dock Two paid for it. That's on me.
The work wasn't unnecessary. The timing was.
And I never want another schedule built around the hope somebody finds a lucky sample.
There's a difference between doing a good job and making a good-looking report.
I can document both without pretending they're identical.
Then that's the report we have, not the one the target wanted.
21: We're sending a missed target with an improved operations record. That's an odd combination.
Are you still hoping they send the bracket?
Every morning. I'm capable of being stubborn and accurate at once.
22: Central is offering us a final choice: meet the output target or submit a different operating proposal.
We already tried making the station fit the target.
This time I'm writing what the station actually is.
